title: Raleigh mother says SNAP benefits delay forced family to use savings as food insecurity rises - ABC11 News
text:
Raleigh mother says SNAP benefits delay forced family to use savings as food insecurity rises - ABC11 Raleigh-Durham 
 24/7 Live Raleigh Durham Fayetteville Surrounding Area SOCIETY 
 Raleigh mom says SNAP delay strained family budget 
 A Raleigh mother says a delay in SNAP benefits created financial hardship for her family as food banks report record levels of need across North Carolina. By Jon Dowding Saturday, October 24, 2026 3:31AM Share RALEIGH, N.C (WTVD) -- A Raleigh mother says a delay in receiving her Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits from Wake County forced her family to drain savings to cover basic needs, as demand for food assistance across central and eastern North Carolina continues to rise.
 Sky Hayden said she submitted the necessary paperwork early for her SNAP benefits review but went a month without receiving assistance. During that time, she said attempts to reach Wake County for answers were unsuccessful.
 "They don't know who else I can reach out to, so I got really frustrated and I reached out to you guys," Hayden said.
 Hayden, a working mother whose daughter has disabilities, said the delay created financial hardship for her family.
 "We had to go into our savings and pretty much deplete that, honestly, in order to be able to catch up and ensure that our daughter has all of the things that she needs," Hayden said.
 Wake County officials said they could not comment on an individual's case. In a statement, the county said:
 "Wake County strives to ensure that all Food and Nutrition Services (FNS) applications and reviews are completed in a timely and accurate manner. While we are meeting timeliness standards for applications, some households may experience delays during reviews. We encourage all households to return their review forms promptly to help avoid delays. Our case managers are working to complete cases as quickly as possible while ensuring accuracy. On average, Wake County processes more than 4,200 FNS applications and more than 3,500 FNS reviews each month."
 Hayden eventually received her benefits after a month of waiting, but her experience comes as the Food Bank of Central & Eastern North Carolina reports record levels of food insecurity.
 "Need is at really record highs, and it's only increasing," said Amy Beros, president and CEO of the Food Bank of Central & Eastern North Carolina. "The need right now is higher than we saw at the height of the pandemic. It's higher than it's been in a generation."
 The Food Bank said many families seeking help are struggling to keep up with rising grocery costs despite being employed or living on fixed incomes.
 "These are families doing everything right. They're working. These are seniors who are living on fixed incomes. It just can't stretch any further," Beros said.

 To meet the growing demand, the organization said it is working with farmers, retailers and community partners to distribute more food, with an emphasis on items that neighbors say are most needed.
 "A specific emphasis on producing protein and produce because that's what our neighbors are saying they need the most. And we also know that's the most expensive when you go to the store," Beros said.
 For Hayden, the experience has created anxiety about the future. She said she is expecting another child and worries about the next benefits review.
 "I am with child, so I have to think about 6 months from now, what that will look like when I have to recertify again, and I have another child in the house who now depends on formula and other various things," Hayden said.
 The Food Bank of Central & Eastern North Carolina encouraged people in need of assistance to contact its community outreach team at 1-800-358-8189 for help finding food resources in the Triangle and surrounding communities.
